purpose: Reconstruct the 2014 Crimea information-environment transformation as a historical defensive reference model for detecting future combinations of infrastructure control, source substitution, propaganda, intimidation and narrative capture.
personal_testimony_policy: No personally identifying travel history or first-hand user testimony is published in this public artifact. First-hand testimony can later be added as a separately consented witness statement; it is not used here to establish facts.
claim_ceiling: Rapid pre-referendum suppression and replacement of major Ukrainian/local broadcast sources and intimidation of journalists are strongly established.
Coordinated pro-Russian narrative framing across Russian official/state media is strongly established.
A rapid radio-layer transformation is supported, but this artifact does not claim every Crimean FM frequency switched in the first days without a frequency-by-frequency reconstruction.
Propaganda was an important operational layer, but outcomes cannot be reduced to propaganda alone; military coercion, prior identities/preferences and institutional capture are major confounders.

timeline.finding: Academic fieldwork describes substantial Russian-language and pro-Russian influence in Crimea before annexation, while Ukrainian national outlets devoted relatively limited local coverage until escalation.
OSCE reported Chernomorskaya television and radio, the peninsula's largest independent broadcaster, taken off air; Crimean authorities also threatened rebroadcasts of Ukrainian channels.
RSF and CPJ reported control/blocking of the Simferopol broadcasting center and the shutdown of Channel 5 and 1+1.
Russian state channels appeared on frequencies used by Ukrainian/local outlets; OSCE listed NTV, Channel One, Rossiya 24, RTR, TNT and Zvezda replacing Ukrainian terrestrial channels.
By the weekend before the referendum, most major Ukrainian terrestrial news channels had been cut or replaced across Crimea/Sevastopol.
OSCE, CPJ and RSF documented assaults, threats, detention, equipment confiscation, denial of access and pressure on independent journalists/media.
The referendum occurred after the major terrestrial source transformation; OSCE said the vote contradicted Ukraine's constitutional framework and did not deploy normal observation.

Russian presidential rhetoric framed Crimea as historical restoration, described the Kyiv transition as a coup involving nationalists/neo-Nazis, invoked protection of Russian speakers and NATO/Sevastopol security concerns.
Public monitoring reported Russian FM brands appearing where Ukrainian stations had ceased broadcasting. Exact first-day frequency mapping remains an open reconstruction task.
Ukrainian channels were removed from major cable networks, followed by raids/licensing pressure and longer-term suppression of independent and Crimean Tatar media.

operational_layers.mechanism: Existing language/identity/media familiarity and pro-Russian local voices
Put Russian state channels on vacated frequencies/cable positions
Intimidation, assault, access denial and outlet pressure
Coup/fascist/Banderite/radical threat; danger to Russian speakers
operational_layers.claim_limit: Real far-right Ukrainian actors existed, but their role was generalized/amplified into an existential characterization.

operational_layers.mechanism: Self-defense, referendum, historical justice, protection, NATO threat
Multiple TV/radio/online/social channels repeat convergent frames rapidly
Dominant news-source set shifts toward Russia-based sources

examples: local self-defense rather than Russian troops
Russia versus fascist/Nazi alternative in campaign imagery

audience_evidence.finding: Before the vote, Ukrainian channels such as Inter and 1+1 still had substantial Crimean news audiences; Russian political-news channels were not the sole dominant source.

USAGM/Gallup reported TV use for news was near-universal in Crimea and later reported that the top five Crimean news sources shifted from Ukrainian in 2012 to Russia-based TV/social sources in spring 2014.
Only a minority reported consciously changing news-gathering habits after Ukrainian channel cessation, consistent with passive source substitution through familiar distribution channels.

relevant_mechanisms: multiple apparent sources increase perceived credibility
high volume can drown out competing messages
emotion and identity-consistent narratives are more transmissible
psychology_model.claim_limit: General persuasion mechanisms do not prove what any specific resident believed because of a given broadcast.

falsifiers_and_confounds: Crimea had genuine pre-existing pro-Russian identities and preferences.
Military presence/coercive control and institutional seizure are independent causal mechanisms.
Ukrainian media had weaknesses in local Crimean coverage before the crisis.
Support measurements after source capture cannot isolate propaganda from coercion, identity, rally effects or perceived interests.
Some Russian claims contained kernels of fact; the propaganda mechanism often involved amplification/generalization rather than pure fabrication.
Radio takeover claims must stay at the granularity actually documented; every-station-immediately remains unproven until a frequency timeline is reconstructed.

transfer_to_tspu_external_warning.historical_pattern: DISTRIBUTION_CONTROL -> SOURCE_REMOVAL -> SOURCE_SUBSTITUTION -> REPETITIVE_THREAT_NARRATIVE -> REDUCED_PLURALISM -> AUDIENCE_ENVIRONMENT_SHIFT
transfer_to_tspu_external_warning.warning: Crimea does not prove exported TSPU will be used this way. It proves Russia has previously integrated information-distribution control with narrative operations during a territorial operation.
transfer_to_tspu_external_warning.measurement_implication: Future monitoring must observe both reachability and source substitution; outage-only detectors can miss information-environment capture.

next_gates: Build a frequency-by-frequency Crimea FM timeline from February through April 2014 using archived spectrum/licensing and broadcaster records.
Code day-level Russian TV narratives from 24 February to 18 March 2014 and compare with physical source-removal events.
Separate narrative appearance, repetition volume, infrastructure substitution and audience uptake into distinct time series.
Use Crimea as a positive historical control and Nicaragua-like surveillance-without-mass-filtering as a negative control.
